issues: In the past, this country had many charitable houses → 此國已往 'from this country onward' (spatial, not temporal) there are many 福舍 (Mizutani: この国より先は)
en_revised: The country of Ṭakka (磔迦國) is over ten thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Vipāśā River to the east and faces the Sindhu River to the west. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much winter wheat; it yields gold, silver, brass, copper, and iron. The climate is hot, and the land is subject to many windstorms. The customs of the people are violent and wicked, and their speech is vulgar and obscene. Their clothing is bright white, consisting of so-called *kauśeya* (silk) garments, *chaoxia* (morning glow) robes, and the like. They have little faith in the Buddhadharma and mostly serve the heavenly deities. There are ten *saṃghārāma*s and several hundred *deva* temples. From this country onward, there are many charitable houses (福舍) to provide for the poor and needy, where medicine or food is distributed; with such provisions for their sustenance, travelers are never in want.

issues: More than ten thousand people → 數萬餘人 'several tens of thousands'; 'Mahirakula' → Mihirakula (spelling made consistent); 未出海島 is read by DM with the preceding clause ('before they had even left the island'); Mizutani attaches it to the following (before [Mihirakula] had left the island, his brother returned) – ambiguous, DM kept
en_revised: Fourteen or fifteen li to the southwest of the great city, one arrives at the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is more than twenty li in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven li in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy and prosperous; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅), who established his capital in this city and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the assembly of monks dared not respond to the command, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, a former servant of the royal household, who had long worn the dyed robes (of a monk), possessed elegant rhetoric and was eloquent and quick in speech, so the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the command. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet you all recommend this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that the wise and brilliant among the monks were comparable to one another, but knowing this now, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and the assembly of monks was to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved and nurtured his people; because of the excessive punishments and tyrannical rule of King Mihirakula, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula prepared his troops to launch a punitive expedition. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, but I shall grant this humble body of mine the chance to slip away into the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and wilds. Several tens of thousands of people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid away on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and set out across the sea to attack. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face; I wish to speak to you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies. Since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You, however, acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unforgivable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya, who was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, was skilled in the art of physiognomy. Hearing that Mihirakula was to be executed, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mihirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mihirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I wear this covering."  The King’s mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; survival and extinction have their destiny. If you equalize things with the mind, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you equalize the mind with things, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times; remove your covering and speak with me, and perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mihirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal enterprise, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will remove my covering to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The King’s mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Shortly after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mihirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and people will look at one another with the pallor of starvation. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother’s command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king’s remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mihirakula (大族王) returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mihirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After much time had passed, he led his people, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed stūpas and abolished saṃghārāmas, totaling one thousand six hundred sites. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprit. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas—do you wish to transmit my evil to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the edge of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, where he will transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a saṃghārāma (伽藍) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasatyasāstra* (勝義諦論) while in this place. Beside it is a stūpa (窣堵波) over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site marking the traces of the four past Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the saṃghārāma, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to transform beings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says: "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."

issues: Before this time, throughout the various regions of India → 此境已往 'from this region onward' (spatial), as far as India the land had no pears or peaches (Mizutani: この境域より先)
en_revised: Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs are timid and weak; the people study both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten *saṃghārāmas* and eight *deva* temples.  In the past, when King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) reigned, his reputation shook neighboring countries and his prestige extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had received the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was his winter residence, and it was therefore called Cīnabhukti. Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  From this region onward and throughout the various regions of India, the land had no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏). For this reason, the people of this country deeply respect the eastern lands, and pointing to one another, they say, "These are the people from the original land of our former king."

issues: Three hundred years after the Nirvāṇa → 第三百年中 'within the third century after'; 數百千 'hundreds of thousands' kept (ambiguous: several hundred or thousand)
en_revised: Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍; Skt. *tamasa-vana*). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their virtuous conduct is lofty. They are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It is said that the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gathered gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. In the third century after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (《發智論》) here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation. Small *stūpas* and various large stone chambers (大石室) stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail. These are all places where sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction; it is difficult to enumerate them all, yet their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of *stūpas* containing the Buddha’s relics, standing so closely that their corners join and their shadows touch.

issues: the forests and trees are lush and sparse → 扶疎 'luxuriant, spreading'; 大小二乘，專門習學 = both vehicles, each studied by its own specialists (DM 'study both' acceptable)
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國). The country of Jālaṃdhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is twelve or thirteen li in circumference. It is suitable for grain crops and has an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests and trees are lush and spreading, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are fierce and unyielding, their appearance is coarse and ugly, and their households are wealthy and prosperous. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas (monasteries) and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are three deva-temples, and more than five hundred followers of non-Buddhist paths, all of whom are ash-smearing ascetics. The former king of this country revered non-Buddhist paths, but later he met an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and enlightenment. Therefore, the king of Mid-India, appreciating his pure faith, entrusted him with the general supervision of all affairs concerning the Three Jewels throughout the five Indias. He made no distinction between his own people and others, forgot preferences and aversions, supervised the monks, and thoroughly investigated their virtues and vices. Consequently, those whose moral conduct was renowned were treated with utmost sincerity and respect, while those whose precepts were violated were severely punished. At all sacred sites, he erected memorial structures, whether stūpas or saṃghārāmas, which are found everywhere throughout the territory of India.

issues: fruits and flowers are plentiful → 果實繁茂 'fruits are plentiful' (no flowers)
en_revised: Traveling south from the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) for over seven hundred li, crossing great mountains and fording a great river, one arrives at the country of Śatadru (設多圖盧國). The country of Śatadru is over two thousand li in circuit and borders a great river to the west. The capital city of the country is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The grain crops are abundant, and fruits are plentiful; it produces much gold and silver, and yields pearls and precious stones. The people’s clothing is fresh and plain, though their garments are elegant and fine. The climate is hot, the customs are honest and harmonious, the people are naturally compliant and obedient, and there is order between those of high and low status. They are devoted to the Buddha-Dharma and are sincere and respectful in their faith. Inside and outside the royal city, there are ten saṃghārāmas, but the courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is very small. Three or four li to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

issues: rests against great mountains (pravaragiri) → 北背大山 'great mountains'; the Sanskrit gloss is invented
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國). The country of Srughna is over six thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā River flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit; it borders the Yamunā River to the east, and although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem merit and wisdom. There are five *saṃghārāmas* with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions seek them out to debate and resolve their doubts. There are one hundred *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā River and outside the eastern gate of a large *saṃghārāma*, there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another *stūpa* containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen *stūpas* containing the hair and nails of the arhats Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and others. After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five *saṃghārāmas* that exist today were built because they were places where masters from other countries debated and triumphed over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.

issues: The arhat… / The heavenly host (天軍) said to him… / requested the heavenly host… the heavenly host, disgusted → 天軍 is the Chinese rendering of the name Devasena (提婆犀那, 唐言天軍 in the Taishō note; Mizutani: 天軍), not a 'heavenly host'; he became deeply concerned → 遂有心焉 'set his mind on it' (to refute it); *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (俱舍雹論) → the work is here called 'Hailstone on the Kośa' (俱舍雹論), only later retitled 順正理論 (Mizutani: Kośakaraka); go and refute Vasubandhu → 以我逸才…逐斥世親 Saṃghabhadra speaks of himself ('I shall drive back'); Saṃghabhadra is not yet dead, and the Master has traveled far → 眾賢未沒，大師遠迹 'while Saṃghabhadra was still alive the Master went far away'
en_revised: Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people value learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities. There are over ten monasteries with more than eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings. There are over fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the śāstra-master Guṇaprabha (瞿拏鉢剌婆) composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The śāstra-master was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory. Originally, he studied the Mahāyāna, but not having fully fathomed its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論), abandoned his former studies, and turned to the Hīnayāna. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahāyāna and establishing the tenets of the Hīnayāna. He also produced several dozen secular works, criticizing and rejecting the treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with great refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (提婆犀那) who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya (慈氏) to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. Devasena (天軍), using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏), he merely bowed and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? Since you wish to receive instruction, how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光) replied, "Venerable one, your words are truly instructive. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys heavenly bliss and is not a companion of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel for hearing the Dharma, did not resolve his doubts even after he had traveled back and forth three times. He again asked Devasena to let him visit Maitreya once more, but Devasena, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not respond. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and immediately went into the mountain forests to practice and develop supernatural powers and meditative concentration; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four li to the north of the Guṇaprabha Monastery (德光伽藍) is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master Saṃghabhadra (眾賢論師) passed away. The master was a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). He was intelligent, learned, and widely known for his reputation since his youth, and he studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) of the Sarvāstivāda school with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親菩薩), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), which was skillful in its phrasing and meaning, and lofty in its reasoning. Saṃghabhadra read and examined it, and thereupon set his mind on refuting it. Thereupon, he delved deeply into his studies with the utmost rigor for twelve years, composing the *Hailstone on the Kośa* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and far-reaching, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and upholding my correct arguments, I shall drive back Vasubandhu (世親) and blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word spread from afar that Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) was coming. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, upon hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must lower yourself to him, we shall be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning judges. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river, while I am old and decrepit, unable to sustain a debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately summoned his companions, shouldered his book satchel, and set out on his long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, but suddenly felt his vitality failing. He thereupon composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, transmitting their respective traditions, each specializing in their own field, favoring those of the same path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) which you composed, I saw that it refuted the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters. Without measuring my own strength, I spent many years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox tradition. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?"  He then carefully selected a disciple who possessed eloquence and told him: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate! I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." As soon as he finished giving these instructions, he suddenly passed away. The disciple took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "My master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for."  Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise. After pondering for a long time, he said to the disciple: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior scholar; although his reasoning was insufficient, his eloquence was abundant. I now wish to refute the treatise of Saṃghabhadra, and it will be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; how much more so when this treatise clarifies my own school?" He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "While Saṃghabhadra was still alive, the Master went far away; having obtained his treatise, to then change its title—how can all the students face the shame of this?" The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to dispel their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a pig and traveling far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, his body was cremated and his bones collected. In the mango grove (āmra-vana) two hundred paces to the northwest of the monastery, a stūpa was erected, which still exists today. Beside the mango grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (毘末羅蜜多羅). The master was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國), who had renounced the world in the Sarvāstivāda school. He was widely versed in the various scriptures and studied heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his life was not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, though a humble student of later generations, have long admired his righteousness and for ages have cherished his virtue." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted the masters of the past; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a mirror, be cautious in your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, indulging in his own biased views, slandered the Mahāyāna and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."

en_revised: In the midst of the Great Snowy Mountains to the north of the borders of this country lies the country of Suvarṇagotra (蘇伐剌拏瞿呾羅國). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women’s Kingdom (東女國). For generations the country has been named after its women. The husband is also a king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men’s only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and severe, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo (吐蕃國), to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan (于闐國), and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha (三波訶國).

For one who is well-manifested, to contemplate… → 夫善現者 '善現' is Subhūti's name (蘇部底) in Chinese: 'It is Subhūti who, contemplating the emptiness of dharmas, has seen the Dharma-body'; tens of thousands of laypeople → 淨人 'monastery servants'; Devāvatāra (三寶階) → 'three precious stairways' (a gloss for the name, the Chinese says three); *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → plain 精舍 'vihāra'
en_revised: More than twenty *li* west of the city is a large monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship exquisite; the sacred forms and venerable images are adorned with the utmost solemnity. There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school, and tens of thousands of monastery servants (淨人) reside in its vicinity. Within the great wall of the monastery are the three precious stairways (三寶階), arranged from north to south and facing east, where the Tathāgata returned from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Jetavana (勝林) and ascended to the heavenly palace, where he resided in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā-sabhā) to preach the Dharma for his mother. After three months had passed, he intended to descend. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, then exercised his divine power to establish a precious stairway: the middle step was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of silver. The Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and, followed by a host of deities, stepped down the middle stairway; the Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, walked on the silver stairway to attend on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped on the crystal stairway to attend on the left; the heavenly host hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues. Several hundred years ago, the stairs still existed, but by the present time, they have completely sunk into the earth. The kings of various countries, lamenting that they could not see them, stacked bricks and stones and decorated them with precious gems upon the original foundation to imitate the ancient precious stairway. It is over seventy feet high, and a *vihāra* (精舍) is built upon it. Inside is a stone Buddha image, and on the stairs to the left and right are images of Śakra and Brahmā, modeled after the original appearance, still in a descending posture. Beside it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its color is dark blue and lustrous, its substance hard and its texture dense. At the top is a lion, crouching and facing the stairway, with strange forms carved and engraved around its four sides; according to the merits or sins of the person, shadows appear within the pillar. Not far from the side of the precious stairway is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata formerly bathed. Beside that is a *vihāra* (精舍), which is the place where the Tathāgata entered into meditation. Beside the *vihāra* is a large stone with a base fifty paces long and seven feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata performed walking meditation. The footprints he trod upon all have lotus flower patterns. To the left and right of the base are small stūpas, which were built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王). In front of the stūpas of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā (蓮華色苾芻尼), wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a Cakravartin king. When the Tathāgata returned to Jambudvīpa from the heavenly palace, Subhūti (蘇部底) was sitting in meditation in a stone chamber and thought to himself: "Now that the Buddha is returning and descending, guided and followed by humans and devas, what is appropriate for someone like me to do? I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-kāya with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a Cakravartin king, guided and followed by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and arrived at the place of the World-Honored One, where she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata said to her: "You are not the first to see me. Subhūti (善現), contemplating that all phenomena are empty, is the one who has seen the Dharma-kāya." Within the enclosure of the holy traces, miraculous manifestations occur one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond; the dragon constantly protects the holy traces. Since there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; although they have decayed naturally over the long years, no human could destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國).

en_revised: The country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city borders the Ganges (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city walls are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions overlooking one another; flower gardens and ponds are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discussions are clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred sanghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks; they study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the time when the people of Kanyakubja were long-lived, their old royal capital was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits and wisdom of the past, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Ganges who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha (尼拘律) fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it grew to provide shade with a trunk of great girth. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the Rishi of the Big Tree (大樹仙人). The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the realm of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard that the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi replied, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander about, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make this request." Hearing his words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your virtue; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (大樹仙人) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed and ordered a carriage to send her to him. Upon arriving at the immortal’s hermitage, the king thanked the immortal, saying, "Great Immortal, you possess supramundane sentiments yet deign to show concern for the worldly; I venture to offer my youngest daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The immortal was displeased upon seeing her and said to the king, "You must despise me as an old man to match me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this youngest one is willing to serve as a maid." The immortal was filled with rage and cast an evil curse, saying, "May the ninety-nine daughters all become hunchbacked at once; with their forms thus ruined and marred, may they remain unmarried for the rest of their lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (曷利沙伐彈那). He rules over the land, being the third king of the second generation. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (波羅羯羅伐彈那), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (曷邏闍伐彈那). Rājyavardhana (王增) succeeded to the throne as the eldest son and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦) of the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) in Eastern India often said to his ministers, "A virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a disaster for one's own kingdom." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and upon meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (婆尼), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided today. The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, state your intentions." The masses all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession passed to Rājyavardhana, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he was abandoned to the hands of his enemies. This is a great shame for the country, and it is the fault of us, your humble ministers. Public opinion and the rumors of the time rightly turn toward your brilliant virtue. If you were to preside over the land, avenge your kin upon the enemy, wash away the shame of the nation, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said: "The weight of national succession has been a difficult matter from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have passed away, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."  He immediately went before the image of the Bodhisattva and, fasting, offered his prayers. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked: "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince replied: "I have only accumulated disasters; my compassionate father has passed away, and I have suffered this heavy, cruel punishment, with my benevolent brother being harmed. Considering myself lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the throne to glorify my father's legacy. I am foolish and ignorant; I dare to hope for your holy instruction!" The Bodhisattva replied: "In a former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting." "By the power of this merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it. Let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the royal lineage, you must follow my instructions; you will be secretly aided by auspicious blessings, and there will be no powerful enemies in the neighboring regions. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King." Thereupon, he received the instruction and withdrew. He immediately succeeded to the throne, calling himself Prince, with the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多). He then said to his ministers: "The vengeance for my brother has not been avenged, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a time to eat with my right hand. All you officials, be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had an elephant corps of 5,000, a cavalry of 20,000, and an infantry of 50,000. Moving from the west to the east, he conquered those who would not submit. The elephants were not unsaddled and the men did not remove their armor; within six years, he brought the five regions of India into submission. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching an elephant corps of 60,000 and a cavalry of 100,000. For nearly thirty years, no weapons were raised in war; the administration and instruction were peaceful. He diligently practiced frugality, seeking merit and cultivating goodness so earnestly that he forgot to sleep or eat. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), he erected several thousand stūpas (窣堵波), each more than one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, streets, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established vihāras (精廬) to store food and drink and provide medicine, distributing these to travelers and the poor without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a saṃghārāma (伽藍). Every five years, he held a great Pañcavārṣika assembly, emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas (沙門) from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the ancient texts were merely treated with respect to show them honor. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to hear of or see them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were different from this, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to be discussed, he would communicate through envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs and did not have a fixed residence, building huts to stay in wherever he arrived. Only during the three months of the rainy season, when there was much rain, did he not travel. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine food to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brāhmaṇas of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had exchanged greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what do you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐) country to seek the Buddha-dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang country lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of li to the northeast of here; it is what the people of India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons and armor rose up in competition, and all living beings were poisoned by suffering. But the Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued and saved all sentient beings, and pacified the world within the seas. His customs and teachings reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The common people, bearing the burden of his nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Battle Lines' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard of this elegant eulogy for a long time. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said?" 'Is this the country of the Great Tang?' I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of the country under our current sovereign. Before he ascended the throne, he was known as the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is called the Son of Heaven. When the destiny of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master; weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with a broad and magnanimous nature, gave rise to a heart of compassion. His majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were brought to peace and quiet, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He cherished and nurtured the four types of birth, revered and honored the Three Jewels, lightened taxes and levies, and reduced punishments and penalties. Yet, the state’s resources remained in surplus, and among the common people there were no dens of crime (無穴). His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully enumerate.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'How magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both water and land. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, which is located in a great flower forest to the west of the Gaṅgā. At that time, more than twenty kings from various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a great monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he had separately constructed a temporary palace. It was then the month of mid-spring. From the first day to the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, exhausted of all adornments; musicians remained in place, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a great elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, and one hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, mixed jewels, and gold and silver flowers as he walked, making offerings to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; the King personally carried the image and escorted it up to the western terrace, making offerings of tens of hundreds of thousands of various jewels and kauśeya garments. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. Each day he escorted the golden image, with the procession following as before, until the final day of the assembly. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a ritual petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if he had extinguished it, the fire and smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and fear increased all the more. Afterward, his expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, and the work of the monastery has been reduced to ashes; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how could we not be grieved? Moreover, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it in this light, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s wishes have been fulfilled; encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata. This is a great good, and there is no cause for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east, ascended the great stūpa, and looked out over the view. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the king. The king, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to step forward to assist. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and ordered that he not be killed. The king personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the greater consequences, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The king asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor this evil intent?" He replied, "Your Majesty has gathered the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide for the śramaṇas and to cast images of the Buddha, yet the heretics who were summoned from afar have not been granted an audience, and they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this treacherous act." Thereupon, the king investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, along with other men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the king's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and assassinate him. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested the execution of the heretics. The king punished the ringleaders but did not incriminate the remaining partisans, banishing the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates. The Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ several thousand households of monastery servants (淨人). In a precious casket in the *vihāra* (精舍), there is a Buddha tooth, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary radiance and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and scholars and commoners gather in great numbers, daily amounting to a hundred thousand, to pay their respects. The overseers, troubled by the clamor and confusion, temporarily established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of pilgrims remains vast, and they pay the gold tax with joyful hearts. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers. Although the flowers pile up, they do not submerge the tooth casket.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there are *vihāras* (精舍) over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers. The Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two temples, there is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the temple, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone temple, there is a shrine to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that shrine, there is a shrine to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are made of polished blue stone and are equally exquisite in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s temple. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without ceasing. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for six months, teaching that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure. Beside it are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; if people are afflicted with illness, they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity and are sure to be cured, receiving their blessings.

issues: Buddhadeva (佛陀馱婆) → the name is Buddhadāsa (Taishō note 唐言覺使 'Buddha's servant'; Mizutani emends 婆 to 娑, Buddhadāsa); arrives at the country → 北至 'arrives north at'
en_revised: From here, traveling eastward for more than three hundred li, one crosses the Ganges (gaṅgā) river and arrives to the north at the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國). The country of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Ganges river and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and their customs are simple; they are diligent in study and fond of merit. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges river, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high; it is the place where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the sitting and walking-meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The pavilions and towers are magnificent, with unique structures rising up; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadāsa (佛陀馱婆) once composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (大毘婆沙論) of the Sarvāstivāda school.

issues: they have sought to make offerings to it, all claiming to have obtained the true image → 遂圖供養，俱言得真 'they had copies (圖) made for worship, each claiming to have the true likeness'; the original is this image (Mizutani: 模写の像を作り); *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → 'vihāra'
en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters fierce beasts and wild elephants that frequently attack travelers; unless one has a large retinue, it is difficult to pass through. Traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國). The country of Kauśāmbī is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much non-glutinous rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous.  Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to carry it away, but although they brought many people, none could move it. Consequently, they had likenesses of it made for worship, each claiming to have obtained the true one; but as to the origin of them all, it is this very image.  Formerly, after the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, remaining there for three months without returning. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others?" "To guide and lead those in the final age, this is truly the hope." More than one hundred paces to the east of the *vihāra* (精舍), there are sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

issues: *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論) → just 'treatise on consciousness-only' (唯識論; not the 成唯識論); *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (顯揚聖教論) → wrong title; 顯揚聖教論 = *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa*
en_revised: In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (具史羅長者). Within it are a Buddhist temple (精舍) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There is also an old foundation that was the bathroom of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed the *Treatise on Consciousness-only* (唯識論) to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery is an old foundation where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa* (顯揚聖教論).  Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of the poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, nothing can be seen there today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country are naturally moved to sorrow, and there are none who do not weep and sigh before returning.

issues: if the assembly of monks were not defeated, they were to cut out their tongues → 眾僧無負，斷舌以謝: if the monks were not defeated, [the heretic] would cut out his tongue (Beal's note: the heretic); Will you recite them in reverse order? → 將覆逆而誦耶 Dharmapāla offers: 'Shall I recite it backwards, or with the words jumbled?'
en_revised: Traveling over seven hundred li through a great forest to the northeast of the dragon cave and crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura (迦奢布羅城), which is over ten li in circuit and whose inhabitants are wealthy and happy. Beside the city is an old monastery of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla once subdued the heretics. A former king of this country supported heterodox views and wished to destroy the Buddha-dharma while venerating the heretics. From among the heretics, he summoned a master of treatises who was intelligent, brilliant, and well-versed in subtle mysteries to compose a fallacious and heterodox work of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, to slander the Buddha-dharma and establish his own sect as the orthodox one. Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. If the heretics were victorious, the Buddha-dharma was to be destroyed; if the assembly of monks were not defeated, [the heretic] would cut out his tongue in atonement. At that time, the monks, fearing defeat, gathered and discussed the matter, saying, "The sun of wisdom has already set, and the bridge of the Dharma is about to be destroyed. The king sides with the heretics; how can we oppose them? With the situation as it is, what plan can we devise?" The assembly was silent, and no one could offer a suggestion. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was eloquent, wise, and widely learned, with a character of great breadth. He spoke out in the midst of the assembly, saying, "Although I am not clever, I ask to present a brief proposal. It is truly appropriate that I should quickly respond to the king's command. If I win the high debate, it will be a spiritual blessing; if I am defeated in the inquiry, it will be attributed to my tender age. In this way, there will be an explanation whether I advance or retreat, and the Dharma and the Sangha will be without fault." Everyone said, "This is acceptable." He followed his plan, immediately responded to the king's command, and ascended the debate seat. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) then laid out his main points, modulating his tone and meaning, and recited his own tenets, waiting for the opponent to raise objections. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) accepted his words and laughed, saying, "I have already won! Shall I recite it in reverse order? Or shall I recite it with the words jumbled?" The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said to him, "Do not be arrogant. If you can repeat the words in their entirety, that will be victory; accept the text as it is, and then explain its meaning." Dharmapāla then followed his intonation and recited the text and its meaning; his phrasing and logic were not in error, and his tone and rhythm were without discrepancy. Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhist wanted to cut out his own tongue. Dharmapāla said, "Cutting the tongue is not an apology; changing one's views is repentance." He then preached the Dharma for him, and his heart became faithful and his mind enlightened. The king abandoned his heterodox path and followed and honored the true Dharma. Beside the place where Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhist, there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has subsided, it is still over two hundred feet high. This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months. Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation (caṅkrama) and a stupa containing his hair and nails.
